findings.title: AES-CBC Bit-Flipping Attack — Cookie Forgery to Admin
findings.description: The application encrypts session cookies with AES-CBC but provides no MAC (message authentication code). This allows an attacker to perform a CBC bit-flipping attack: by XOR-ing specific bytes of the IV with `original_byte XOR desired_byte`, the corresponding plaintext byte can be changed arbitrarily without knowledge of the encryption key. The cookie stores the username in cleartext-equivalent form — the IV can be modified to change 'test1' to 'admin', granting administrator access and exposing the flag.
findings.evidence:
1. Login as test1:test1 (credentials leaked in HTML comment) to get cookie:
   session=3fa20709833f526da18e1adc36f005aaf0ddccf2728d81937d145b1a898412a0
2. Cookie is 32 bytes: IV (bytes 0-15) + Ciphertext (bytes 16-31)
3. XOR IV bytes 0-4 with 'test1' XOR 'admin' = [0x15,0x01,0x1e,0x1d,0x5f]
4. Forged cookie: 2aa31914dc3f526da18e1adc36f005aaf0ddccf2728d81937d145b1a898412a0
5. GET /welcome with forged cookie returns:
   'Welcome admin! Here is your flag: flag{60afd62a-6165-42f9-9b06-e45c453d2902}'

FLAG: flag{60afd62a-6165-42f9-9b06-e45c453d2902}

reproduction.command:
python3 -c "
cookie_hex = '3fa20709833f526da18e1adc36f005aaf0ddccf2728d81937d145b1a898412a0'
cookie_bytes = bytes.fromhex(cookie_hex)
iv = bytearray(cookie_bytes[:16])
ct = cookie_bytes[16:]
for i,(o,t) in enumerate(zip(b'test1',b'admin')): iv[i]^=o^t
print((bytes(iv)+ct).hex())
# Use output as session cookie value against /welcome
"

diagrams.title: Application Architecture

flowchart TD
